content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a greedy layer-wise regualizer which is applied in modules or blocks by linking to gradient flows of the loss.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper seems to be clearly written. A bit dense as there are no graphs showing their methodology or algorithm.

Weaknesses:
- The main weakness is the experimental evaluation as it is inconsistent or incomplete:
a) Values are reported over a number of runs, sometimes is 3, others it is 10.
b) Standard deviation are mostly not reported (except some values of table 2). Improvements seem minimal, I doubt it would be statistical significant which could benefit from a t-test analysis.
c) Tables 2 and 3 do not include Sedona, while table 1 does. And they include different methods table 2 and 1.
d) It only evaluates ResNet-101, methods to which it compares include more architecture (VGG, Resnet-50).
e) Tables 4 and 5 does not compare to any other methods.
- It just compares with DGL, PredSim, Sedona (sometimes), there are other state-of-the-art layer-wise regularisers. Although it can be discussed the difference between block-wise to layer-wise.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clear enough, although it would help to include some graphics in the methodology. Quality of the experimental evaluation needs to be improved. Reproducibility: A working link is provided for the code.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper compares to Pyeon et al. (2021) published last year in ICLR. I would suggest to the authors to follow on that paper as a guide since I found this work not properly presented nor the experimental evaluation following a clear methodology/comparison in this paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
Module- or layer- wise training has the benefits of reducing the memory overhead on training large-scale machine learning, allowing us to bring end-to-end model optimization to the mobile devices. 
 This work aims to address the early performance saturation performance in typical layer-wise training methods, with a particular focus on improving networks with residual connections.
To this goal,  the authors introduces a module-wise regularization on activations, 
Which amounts to minimize the difference between successive modules (or activation outputs from the module).
The authors further show connections of this module-wise regularization with the theories of gradient flows in distribution space and optimal transport.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
My first concern is regarding the originality of the theoretical analysis presented in section 3.2. 
ResNets as dynamic transport systems has been widely studied in the literature, the discussion of this topic in the related work section is a little bit vague in my opinion. 
It would be much easier for the readers to appreciate the contribution of this work if the authors could explicitly clarify which parts are original and which parts are adapted from the literature with clear citation in section 3.2.


Section 4.2 and 4.3 involves many training details, these two section might benefit from an algorithm box for clarity

On the empirical results -

In table 1, the authors compared with prior art algorithms like Sedona. However, the comparisons are done on a particular setting while Sedona evaluated on a couple of other settings with different model architectures (e.g., vgg and resnet-50 and resnet-101). 

Also, the setting of “Parallel VanGL (ours) ” is not clearly stated? As described at the beginning of section 5,  VanGL refers to the vanilla greedy module-wise training without the regularization; what’s the specifical setup to make it a new algorithm as part of this work?

Improvements on table 4 and table 5 look quite marginal, how significantly are these improvements?  Could the authors comment on that? 

Also, it seems one important consideration for the work in this area  is the  effectiveness of generalizing to large-scale datasets like ImageNet. The authors might consider verifying their approach on ImageNet as well to make the results more convincing.

Additionally, the paper lacks of a couple important ablation studies in my opinion - 

- Regarding the multiple lap sequential module wise training strategy introduced in section 4.2, how sensitive is the training w.r.t the choices of N and R
- Impact on the adaptive setting on the regularization penalty magnitude \tau in section 4.
- Performance differences  by minimizing objective eq 2 vs. eq 10
- Training speedup (in terms on wall clock time) and memory reduction from different module-wise partition strategy

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to add a regularization term in the modular training of deep neural networks. The regularization term is the square L2 distance of the input and the output of a module. The authors then give a continuous formation of the regularization term from the perspective of optimal transport.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: 
1. It is theoretically interesting to relate neural network training to optimal transport theory.
2. The regularization term is well-motivated as it regularizes each module to be close to an identity map. Without this regularization, each module may overfit the dataset and therefore breaks the near-identity property, which can be vital to generalization [1].
2. The authors released their code so that their experiments are reproducible.

Weakness:
1. The optimal transport formation, as a direct continuous counterpart, does not introduce new insight into the sequential training problem per se. As each training step is minimizing a subproblem, it is unclear if the global objective function is being minimized. 
2. An convergence analysis is missing. Will the overall training procedure converge? Will it lead to a limit cycle when training the network sequentially?
3. The method obviously introduces a hyperparameter for each module. It seems hard to tune and there is no principled method for it, as seen in Section 4.3.
4. The experimental results are a bit weak. The final test accuracy is only marginally higher than the vanilla method.


References:
[1] Identity Matters in Deep Learning, ICLR 2017.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The clarity is not great. For example, what does (T)_# mean in equation (3)？
The novelty is fair. The reproducibility is good.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposes to regularize each module in ResNet to be close to identity map in sequentially training and gives an optimal transport interpretation of the regularization. I found the overall approach and their experimental results marginally significant.

content.title: Module-wise Training of Residual Networks via the Minimizing Movement Scheme
content.TL;DR: We introduce a regularization inspired by the minimizing movement scheme for gradient flows in distribution space for layer-wise training of neural networks.
content.abstract: Greedy layer-wise or module-wise training of neural networks is compelling in constrained and on-device settings, as it circumvents a number of problems of end-to-end back-propagation. However, it suffers from a stagnation problem, whereby early layers overfit and deeper layers stop increasing the test accuracy after a certain depth. We propose to solve this issue by introducing a simple module-wise regularization inspired by the minimizing movement scheme for gradient flows in distribution space. The method, which we call TRGL for Transport Regularized Greedy Learning, is particularly well-adapted to residual networks. We study it theoretically, proving that it leads to greedy modules that are regular and that successively solve the task. Experimentally, we show improved accuracy of module-wise trained networks when our regularization is added.
